Attitude adverbials
Attitude adverbials consist of a word or phrase which: 
s� is normally placed at the beginning of the sentence
s� is normally followed by a comma (see Using commas on 
page 121)
s� expresses the writer’s attitude to what he/she is going to 
say in the sentence: Surprisingly , many people believe 
that dogs cannot see colours . (The writer is saying he 
ﬁ nds it surprising that many people believe this.)
Attitude adverbials may express:
s� a feeling or emotion: 
Sadly, few students have applied for the grant .
s� a context: 
Generally speaking , grants are only given to post-
graduate students. 
Of course, this is not true in all cases .
s� an attitude:
Frankly, I think people should take more care of their 
pets.
s� an opinion: 
As far as I’m concerned , all public buildings should be 
decorated in bright colours .
s� emphasis: 
As a matter of fact , colour blindness is more common 
among men than women. 
Actually, it affects about 8% of men in North America, 
whereas only 0.5% of women are affected .
Attitude adverbials can sometimes come between the object 
and the verb. Note the use of commas before and after the 
adverbial when it is not in the usual position in the sentence:
He was, surprisingly , very upset = Surprisingly , he was 
very upset. 
Dependent prepositions
Many verbs, nouns and adjectives are followed by a 
particular preposition: 
In his lecture, Dr Patel focused on genetic variations in fruit 
ﬂ i e s.
There are no clear rules to help you decide which 
preposition should follow a particular word; the best 
strategy is to learn the preposition with the word.
You should use a dictionary to check how words and 
prepositions are used. Look at this example from the 
Cambridge Advanced Learner’s Dictionary (CALD):
apologize, UK USUALLY apologise /ə/vertstrokesuperiorpɒ.lə.dȝaiz/ /ə/vertstrokesuperiorpɑ/lengthmarklə.dȝaiz/ verb [I] 
to tell someone that you are sorry for having done something that has caused 
them inconvenience or unhappiness:
I must 
apologize to Isobel for my lateness.
She apologized profusely for having to leave at 3.30 p.m.
The examples show that you can apologise for something 
which went wrong. You apologise to the person you are 
addressing.
Remember: a preposition must be followed by a noun, noun 
phrase, pronoun or verb + -ing:

Task 1 (Academic) – Overview & Tips
Always overview the main trend (increase, decrease, stability).
Use comparative language:
“The number of X was higher than Y.”
“Sales of A rose signiﬁcantly, whereas sales of B declined.”
Don’t describe every number → focus on trends.
Use variety of words: increase = rise, climb, grow, soar.
Academic Task 1
You’ll be given a visual input such as:
Bar chart
Line graph
Pie chart
Table
Map
Process diagram
Your job: summarize the information in at least 150 words.
What examiners expect:
Overview: a summary of the most signiﬁcant trends or features (don’t list every single 
number).
Comparisons: highlight differences and similarities.
Clarity: organize information logically.
Accuracy: describe changes and trends using the right words.
Tips to Score High in Academic Task 1:
Always write an overview: Identify the biggest trend or most striking feature. For 
example, “Overall, sales of smartphones rose dramatically, while landline usage fell 
sharply.”

Common Mistakes to Avoid in IELTS Writing
Not Answering the Question Directly
Mistake: Writing everything you know about the topic, but not focusing on what the task 
is asking.
Why it hurts: Examiners mark you down for Task Achievement.
Fix: Underline keywords in the question. Always rephrase the question in your 
introduction to stay on track.
Overusing Basic Vocabulary
Mistake: Repeating “good,” “bad,” “important,” “very,” etc.
Why it hurts: Shows limited range of vocabulary.
Fix: Use synonyms (e.g., crucial, signiﬁcant, beneﬁcial instead of important).
Writing Like a Text Message
Mistake: Using contractions (don’t, can’t, won’t), informal words (kids, stuff, a lot).
Why it hurts: IELTS Writing needs formal academic style.
Fix: Write do not, cannot, children, many, things instead.
Too Short or Too Long
Mistake: Writing under 150 words (Task 1) or 250 words (Task 2), or going over 400 words.
Why it hurts: Too short = not enough ideas. Too long = more mistakes, less time.
Fix: Aim for 170–190 words (Task 1) and 260–290 words (Task 2).
Forgetting Paragraphing
Mistake: Writing one giant block of text.
Why it hurts: Examiners can’t see a clear structure = lower Coherence & Cohesion score.

Fix: Always use 4–5 paragraphs (Intro, 2–3 Body, Conclusion).
Misusing Linking Words
Mistake: Overusing moreover, furthermore, in addition in every sentence.
Why it hurts: Sounds mechanical, not natural.
Fix: Mix them naturally (also, besides, on top of that, what’s more).
Spelling & Grammar Slips
Mistake: Writing “goverment” instead of “government,” or using wrong tenses.
Why it hurts: Lowers Lexical Resource & Grammar score.
Fix: Always leave 3 minutes at the end to check spelling and basic grammar.
No Clear Opinion (Task 2)
Mistake: Sitting on the fence, never choosing a side.
Why it hurts: The examiner can’t tell what your position is.
Fix: Choose a side clearly, even if you “partly agree.” Always restate your opinion in the 
conclusion.
Memorized Phrases / Copy-Paste
Mistake: Writing generic templates like “Since the beginning of time, people have argued 
about…”
Why it hurts: Examiners can spot memorized sentences instantly.
Fix: Use ﬂexible sentence starters, not clichés.
Spending Too Long on Task 1
Mistake: Writing Task 1 for 30+ minutes, then rushing Task 2.
Why it hurts: Task 2 is worth double the marks.
Fix: Stick to 20 minutes for Task 1, 40 minutes for Task 2.
Closing Thoughts on Writing
The IELTS Writing test can feel like the hardest part of the exam, but remember this: it’s not 
about being a perfect writer, it’s about being a clear and effective communicator. Examiners 
don’t expect you to sound like Shakespeare or a published author — they want organized 
ideas, logical arguments, and academic tone.
If you:
Understand the task requirements,
Plan your ideas before writing,
Use a wide range of vocabulary and grammar, and
Avoid the common mistakes we’ve covered,
…then you’re already on track to hit Band 7 or higher.

Writing takes practice, but it’s also a skill you can train with the right strategy. Stay consistent, 
keep reviewing your essays, and don’t be afraid to get feedback.
Next up, let’s dive into the part that most people are nervous about: Speaking 
IELTS Speaking
The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner. It lasts around 11–14 minutes 
and is divided into 3 parts. Many test-takers feel nervous here, but remember: the examiner is 
not your enemy. Their job is to give you a chance to show your English skills.
Structure of the Speaking Test
Part 1: Introduction & Interview (4–5 minutes)
The examiner asks you about familiar topics (home, work, studies, hobbies, hometown, 
daily life).
Goal: Show natural, conﬁdent answers to simple questions.
Example: “What do you usually do on weekends?”
Part 2: Long Turn (3–4 minutes)
You’ll get a cue card with a topic.
You have 1 minute to prepare, then speak for up to 2 minutes.
Goal: Organize your ideas with a clear beginning, middle, and end.
Example cue card: “Describe a book you recently read.”
Part 3: Discussion (4–5 minutes)
The examiner will ask you deeper, abstract questions related to Part 2.
Goal: Show critical thinking, opinions, and the ability to explain with examples.
Example: “Do you think reading habits have changed in the digital age?”

Be natural, not memorized → Examiners can tell if you’re reciting.
Expand your answers → Don’t just say “Yes/No.” Give reasons and examples.
Use linking phrases → “In my opinion, to be honest, as a matter of fact, on top of that…”
Pronunciation matters → It’s about clarity, not accent.
Fluency > Perfection → Better to speak smoothly with small mistakes than to pause too 
much.

Sleep is often underestimated in modern society, where long working hours and constant 
digital distractions are common. Yet scientists argue that sleep is just as essential as food and 
water for human survival. On average, adults require between seven to nine hours of sleep

For thousands of years, climate has shaped the development of human civilization. Shifts in 
rainfall, temperature, and natural disasters have inﬂuenced agriculture, migration, and even

IELTS Writing Practice – Task 2 (Problem & Solution)
Question:
 In many large cities around the world, traffic congestion has become a major problem.
 What are the main causes of this issue, and what solutions can you suggest?
Write at least 250 words.
Band 7–8 Sample Answer
Traffic congestion is one of the most pressing challenges in urban areas today. With the rapid 
growth of cities, many people experience longer commuting times and lower quality of life 
due to crowded roads. This essay will discuss the main causes of traffic congestion and 
suggest possible solutions.
One major reason for heavy traffic is the increasing number of private vehicles. As cities 
develop, more people can afford to buy cars and motorcycles, which puts pressure on 
existing road networks. Additionally, in many cities, public transportation systems are either 
unreliable or insufficient. Without an efficient alternative, commuters naturally prefer to 
drive, further worsening congestion. Another contributing factor is poor urban planning. In 
some places, residential and business districts are far apart, forcing individuals to travel long 
distances every day.
There are several measures that can be taken to address this problem. Firstly, governments 
should invest in reliable and affordable public transport, such as subways, buses, and light 
rail systems. If people have convenient alternatives, they are less likely to depend on private 
cars. Secondly, authorities could introduce policies such as congestion charges or higher 
parking fees to discourage unnecessary car use in city centers. Finally, promoting ﬂexible 
working arrangements, like remote work or staggered office hours, could reduce peak-time 
traffic.
In conclusion, the problem of traffic congestion is mainly caused by the overuse of private 
vehicles and inadequate urban planning. However, by improving public transportation, 
implementing stricter policies, and encouraging ﬂexible work practices, cities can 
signiﬁcantly reduce traffic and create a better living environment for their residents.

Disadvantages)
Question:

commuting to an office every day.
 Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?

Band 7–8 Sample Answer
The rise of technology and remote communication tools has made working from home 
increasingly common. While this trend has both positive and negative aspects, I believe the 
advantages generally outweigh the disadvantages.
On the one hand, working from home offers several beneﬁts. Firstly, employees save 
signiﬁcant time and money by avoiding long commutes. This not only reduces stress but also 
allows individuals to achieve a better work–life balance. Secondly, remote work can boost 
productivity, as people can create personalized work environments and concentrate without 
office distractions. Moreover, from an environmental perspective, fewer commuters mean 
less traffic congestion and lower carbon emissions.
On the other hand, there are some drawbacks to this trend. One major issue is the lack of 
social interaction. Working remotely may lead to feelings of isolation and reduced teamwork, 
which can affect collaboration and creativity. Another concern is blurred boundaries between 
personal and professional life. Some employees ﬁnd it difficult to “switch off” after work, 
leading to overworking and burnout. Additionally, not all professions are suitable for remote 
work, so inequality may arise between those who can and cannot beneﬁt from this option.
In conclusion, despite the disadvantages of social isolation and blurred work–life boundaries, 
the advantages of remote work, such as time savings, reduced stress, and environmental 
beneﬁts, make it a largely positive development. With proper support systems and company 
policies, the drawbacks can be minimized, allowing both employees and employers to beneﬁt.

 Others argue that students should pay for their own studies.

Band 7–8 Sample Answer
There has been much debate about whether higher education should be provided free of 
charge. While some argue that free education beneﬁts society as a whole, others believe 
students must take ﬁnancial responsibility for their studies. This essay will examine both 
perspectives before presenting my own opinion.
Supporters of free university education often point out that it promotes equality. Students 
from disadvantaged backgrounds would have the same opportunities as wealthier peers, 
ensuring that talent, not ﬁnancial status, determines success. Moreover, educated citizens 
contribute more effectively to the economy, pay higher taxes, and improve innovation, which 
beneﬁts the entire country.
On the other hand, critics argue that making universities free would place a heavy burden on 
taxpayers. They believe that individuals who directly beneﬁt from education should invest in 
it themselves. Additionally, tuition fees can motivate students to take their studies more 
seriously, as they have a ﬁnancial stake in their education.
In my view, while complete free education may not be ﬁnancially sustainable, governments 
should at least subsidize or partially fund higher education. This would ensure access for 
capable students without creating unsustainable pressure on national budgets.
In conclusion, although free university education has clear advantages in terms of equality, a 
balanced approach, where costs are shared between governments and students, seems the 
most practical solution.
